name: streamvbyte-simdgo
baseline: Go encoding/binary Uvarint/PutUvarint (LEB128 varint), via the repo's util.GetVarint/PutVarint wrappers
workload: Decoding and encoding uint32 arrays (8 values per call, and streamed counts 1e0 to 1e7) with Stream VByte (AVX/AVX2 assembly) versus Go's standard varint loop.
claimed_speedup: README table: Get8uint32Fast 10095.99 MB/s vs Get8uint32Varint 731.10 MB/s decode (about 13.8x, derived from page data); ReadAllFast Count_1e6 5490.62 MB/s vs ReadAllVarint Count_1e6 695.04 MB/s (about 7.9x, derived from page data); delta variants Get8uint32DeltaFast 7183.20 MB/s vs Get8uint32DeltaVarint 558.46 MB/s. Encode: Put8uint32Fast 8281.18 MB/s vs Put8uint32Varint 1860.67 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain, default go test -bench flags; Go version not stated in README (go.mod says go 1.16)
tradeoffs: Stream VByte format (separate control and data streams), not LEB128 compatible. SIMD path needs x86_64 with AVX/AVX2 (runtime check, scalar fallback). Not usable from C++ directly; the C++ reference is lemire/streamvbyte, which is already catalogued.
caveats: Benchmark code is in the repo (pkg/decode/decode_test.go, pkg/encode, pkg/stream) and the README table can be reproduced, but Go version is not stated and the machine is a single laptop-class macOS i7. Microbenchmarks on 8 values. The slow side is Go's own scalar varint; no comparison to the C reference or to other Go SIMD codecs. Last commit is 2021-09-12.
found_via: WebSearch: 'stream-vbyte Rust OR Go OR Java github Stream VByte implementation faster than varint'; github.com/topics/integer-compression

name: JavaFastPFOR
baseline: VariableByte (the varint scheme included in the same library) and Kamikaze PForDelta
workload: Compressing and decompressing sorted-gap integer arrays (benchmark run at sparsity 1, 2, ...), reporting bits per int and millions of ints per second; Java port of the FastPFor C++ library.
claimed_speedup: benchmarkresults_icore7_10may2013.txt, sparsity 1, decompression: IntegratedBinaryPacking+IntegratedVariableByte 1183 mis, FastPFOR+VariableByte 811 mis, versus VariableByte 299 mis and Kamikaze PForDelta 262 mis (about 4x and 2.7x over VariableByte, derived from page data); README says over 1.2 billion ints per second (4.5 GB/s) decode and that Kamikaze PForDelta is slower than these codecs.
hardware: Core i7 (from the result file name 'icore7', exact model not stated), 2013
stars_or_usage: 569 stars; used in LinkedIn Pinot, Apache NiFi, Terrier (per README); modified parts in Parquet and Lucene
tradeoffs: JVM only; usable from C++ only by using the C++ FastPFor instead (already catalogued). Integrated (delta) codecs need sorted input. Development versions need JDK 21 or later.
caveats: Result file is from 2013 on an unspecified i7 and JVM; no JVM flags stated. The variable-byte baseline is the library's own VariableByte, not a third-party varint. Numbers on that page are in a text dump, so the ratios are derived. The C++ project it ports is already catalogued; this entry is for the Java port.
found_via: WebSearch: 'JavaFastPFOR OR Simple8b Go github integer encoding SIMD faster benchmark timestamps compression'

name: zint
baseline: LZ4 and Zstandard level 1 (plain memcopy as the ceiling); no varint, Simple8b or FastPFor comparison
workload: Compress and decompress synthetic u8 to u128 arrays (bit width 7, 15, 32; plain, delta and frame-of-reference variants; lengths 10 to 262144) with FastLanes-based bitpacking, versus lz4, zstd(1) and memcopy.
claimed_speedup: epyc9354.txt, T=u32, DATASET=width7, LENGTH=123321: zint_bitpack decompress 26.931GB/s, compress 29.128GB/s versus lz4 decompress 3.811GB/s, zstd(level 1) decompress 0.907GB/s and memcopy 15.429GB/s; width15 same length: zint_bitpack decompress 21.353GB/s versus lz4 9.016GB/s and zstd 2.436GB/s. README: right variant is 'massively faster than lz4 or zstd' and almost matches memcopy.
compiler_and_flags: zig build bench -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (Makefile); build.zig.zon minimum_zig_version 0.16.0-dev.732+2f3234c76; actual Zig version used is not recorded in the result file
hardware: AMD EPYC 9354 (inferred from file name epyc9354.txt; a second file ryzen7600x.txt exists); CPU model is not printed in the file
tradeoffs: Zig library, not callable from C++ without a C wrapper. Based on a port of spiraldb's Rust FastLanes layout, which is not binary compatible with the original FastLanes. Fixed 1024-element blocks; delta variant is slower than memcopy. Safe on untrusted input.
caveats: Compares against general-purpose lz4 and zstd, not against varint, Simple8b or FastPFor, so it does not show a win over the category baselines. Synthetic datasets. CPU model and Zig version come from file names and build.zig.zon, not from the result file. At very short lengths (10 to 69 elements) zint is slower than lz4 and memcopy. Author's own benchmark.
found_via: WebSearch: 'spiraldb fastlanes OR fastlanez bitpacking Rust Zig github FFOR delta unpack'

name: dennwc/varint
workload: Decoding protobuf-style varints of 1 to 9 bytes, plus UvarintSize, per call in ns/op.
claimed_speedup: README benchstat: Uvarint/1 3.46 to 2.64 ns/op (-23.73%), Uvarint/4 8.04 to 3.54 ns/op (-55.97%), Uvarint/8_large 14.1 to 4.89 ns/op (-65.43%); UvarintSize/5 4.29 to 0.57 ns/op (-86.71%).
tradeoffs: Same LEB128/protobuf wire format as the standard library, so it is a drop-in decoder; scalar code, no bulk or SIMD path. Go only.
caveats: README shows only a benchstat diff: CPU model, Go version and flags are not stated (the -8 suffix is GOMAXPROCS). Per-integer microbenchmark, not bulk throughput. This is a plain varint decoder, a marginal fit for the bitpacking category.
found_via: github.com/topics/varint page; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: chmike/varint
workload: Encoding and decoding single unsigned integers of 7 to 63 bits with a big-endian prefix-code varint, ns/op.
claimed_speedup: docs/data.txt: at 63 bits the prefix-code encoder takes about 2.992 ns/op versus 5.051 ns/op for the standard library encoder; at 7 bits both are comparable (about 0.69 ns/op for this library); README says LEB128 is significantly slower for values above 35 bits.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-11400 @ 2.60GHz, Linux amd64 (from docs/data.txt header)
tradeoffs: Different wire format (prefix code, most significant byte first), incompatible with LEB128 and protobuf; the speedup appears mainly for large values. Go only.
caveats: Numbers were read through a page summary of docs/data.txt and the README graphs, not re-derived from the raw file; Go version is not stated. Win is limited to large values (over about 35 bits), and no win at 7 bits. Marginal fit for the bitpacking category.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github varint decode SIMD AVX2 OR NEON OR BMI2 PrefixVarint OR LEB128 faster than protobuf varint library benchmark'
